claims.text: The target nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially form a single-phase solid solution.
Kinetic limitations, rather than thermodynamic high-entropy stabilization alone, can govern multimetal nanoparticle stability.
Under electrocatalytic conditions, dissolution kinetics can overcompensate thermodynamic contributions to multinary-alloy stability.
Surface atomic diffusion specifically governs structural and chemical stability throughout 473–1923 K under both catalytic and thermoelectric operation.
A surface kinetic barrier can slow atomic rearrangement and dissolution that would otherwise produce phase segregation.
Graphene shells can be formed around CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Encapsulation and non-encapsulation constitute the controlled comparison, with composition and operating protocol otherwise held identical.
The comparison is to be conducted under inert or controlled atmospheres while temperatures are ramped within 473–1923 K.
Elevated temperature increases intrinsic atomic mobility and thereby promotes surface diffusion and elemental migration.
Surface diffusion and elemental migration can cause phase separation or chemical degradation in these nanoparticles.
A graphene shell slows surface diffusion sufficiently to preserve the initial solid-solution structure.
Thermodynamic driving forces may favor segregation at high temperature even when segregation is kinetically delayed.
Encapsulated nanoparticles will segregate and dissolve more slowly than otherwise identical unencapsulated nanoparticles.
Encapsulation will better preserve single-phase structure and catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
The hypothesis is limited to conditions in which surface diffusion is the primary degradation pathway.
Strong oxidation, abrupt phase transitions, bulk diffusion, or other unmitigated chemical reactions may override the effect of surface encapsulation.
Similar segregation, migration, and degradation rates in encapsulated and unencapsulated samples would falsify the proposed kinetic-barrier mechanism.
